Question: I have an LG Netcast TV from 2009. I'm connected, but it shows an error. Why was Netcast discontinued?
Answer: When you're writing apps for TV platforms you have to maintain the apps for the maximum number of viewers. We have to write for LG webOS, Tizen, Panasonic, Android TV, etc. and app development isn't static, you're always having to tweak it and make changes just for maintenance let alone improvements. So, as a TV platform becomes less used it becomes harder to justify the effort of maintaining the app on it. The audience on Netcast has been falling away for a long while. Then you encounter the problem that what you want to do with the app becomes harder and harder on these old devices because their capabilities just aren't up there with what's baseline today (not talking about state of the art, just baseline). So then you're effectively asking to write two different apps, a limited capability app and your main product for everyone else. Then that means you as a user are getting a worse experience than we'd like and some of the things we're advertising, you can't get. So we'll get complaints about the app on Netcast not being what was advertised, it's a confusing message to market. From LGs perspective, they don't make money from those TVs. Manufacturers barely make money selling TVs and many brands will lose money selling a TV. Then because it's an internet connected device it's going to need software updates to keep working, for example just keeping the security certificates current. Part of the online services is paid for by partnerships with the apps, the TV manufacturers sometimes get a kickback for each sign-up via their TV or pay-per-view purchases. That revenue just about pays for the connected TV maintenance. Once a platform loses audience the effort needed to maintain the platform exceeds the revenue. Remember, you're not paying LG and they have to maintain servers running 24/7 ready for your TV. So, the reason Netcast was discontinued was that maintenance costs were no longer justifiable.

Question: How does IPTV handle simultaneous streaming during popular live sports events?

Question: How is the direction of a TV show or a sport event (made for example in Italy) shared all over the world to multiple TV broadcasters?
Answer: For a sports event there will be a production crew at the stadium that will create what is called the “World Feed” which is the generic version of the event not intended to target any one language. Then that world feed can be distributed via fibre (or satellite but that’s reducing) from the venue out to the various broadcasters. There are plenty of different telecoms providers and when you work with a stadium you learn which ones provide video connectivity. While it can be done over the internet, more often than not it’s going to be a private video circuit from the stadium to a connection point. Then you as a broadcaster have to figure out what partner provides you can use to get it from A to B. Increasingly this is being done over the internet but for major events, private circuits are still the way to go for their high quality and high reliability. As a major broadcaster you’ll have teams of people who know how to get a video signal from anywhere to anywhere around the world. When the world feed gets back to your studios you can add local commentary and graphics on to it, insert your own promotional videos or ads, then broadcast it. If you’re not just interested in the world feed and want something more custom. Then as a broadcaster you’ll have your own production team at the stadium, they’ll still probably take the world feed, but may also bring one or two cameras of their own for things like on-site interviews, on-site commentary or views from the sidelines. Then you’ll either have your own team doing the mixing/production on-site, or you can send the world feed, along with your raw on-site production video back to your base and they can mix the video there. The Olympics is considered the apex of this process, there’s an entire company called “Olympic Broadcast Services” (OBS) whose job it is to build an entire TV production centre around the Olympics that allows any licensed broadcaster to take a feed from any event and replays/recordings of most events in case they missed something. Then each broadcaster can either just use the raw material, or shoot their own extra material using their own resources. The important thing is that you can’t have a dozen different companies all wanting to do their own full production for a sporting event. Everyone has to take the world feed and then they can do what they want on the side as long as it doesn’t interfere.

Name: Bob Hannent
Question: How is a TV programme conveyed from the studio, videotape or film to the transmitter? Was it done the same way as now when TV first started? How are programmes conveyed to relay transmitters? How is regional programming in a network coordinated?
Answer: A pre-recorded TV programme is not likely to be handled on tape anymore. It will be done entirely digitally. Sometimes media is delivered on SSDs or memory cards, but more often these days you're going to use a file transfer over the internet. One of the most popular tools for this amongst broadcasters is IBM Aspera. Either the production company has an Aspera licence or the broadcaster will, and then you use the Aspera tool to upload your media files along with documentation about it. Then that gets checked by someone for Quality Control (QC), before being loaded into a Media Asset Management system (MAM). It could go straight from Aspera to the MAM, and then get checked for QC while stored in the MAM but that's just process. From the MAM it'll get scheduled to be broadcast in their scheduling system. Then the video will be loaded into the Playout system. That's an application on a server that plays all the media that a channel needs. There might also then be a ‘presentation mixer’ which is where a presentation controller (who is a person) can switch between different playout systems or switch to a live sources (like a live studio or event). Then the output of presentation will be the channel, with all it's fancy graphics and advertising. From Presentation it goes to Coding and Multiplexing, which is where it's compressed and multiple channels get aggregated together. From there, it will go over fibre (some folk here say microwave but that's just a backup in my world) to the transmitter sites. Then it gets converted to a broadcast radio signal and big amplifiers boost the signal before it goes up the mast to the antenna. In the old days there may have been operators at the transmitter who looked at the video, but that's largely redundant now and transmitters can be remotely controlled.

Question: How can movie theaters be made quieter without affecting audio quality and improving the overall viewing experience?

Question: Why does Netflix have different content for each country, even though it is owned by the same company?
Answer: Netflix doesn't make all its content, even the content that has it's name on it can be what's called a ‘co-production’. So in different markets there will be different deals that have been struck for content. In some markets Warner Bros Discovery, or Sony might do a deal which provides them exclusivity for a show/series/film. Each company's regions will be bidding on the rights for different shows and at different times, sometimes there could be a global deal and overlapping deals, but sometimes there's local exclusivity. One funny example is that in the UK, Disney wouldn't/couldn't launch Disney+ because the biggest satellite TV company (Sky) owned the local rights to one of Disney's key shows (I can't remember, it might have been Toy Story or Minions). Rather than dilute their offering in the UK, Disney decided to delay the product launch for their + service until the rights deal had expired. In a co-production, multiple companies will throw money into the pot to make a show/film/series and in exchange they get some agreed rights. Classically the BBC will do a deal with German and French broadcasters, perhaps also PBS, and they'd produce some spectacular nature or drama programme. Then each national broadcaster gets the rights to it in their own territory. Now we have global platforms like Netflix, Netflix might buy the global right for some content, but in the UK it could still be exclusive for the BBC (for example). There can even be things like, a broadcaster has the right to broadcast a show the traditional way but cannot provide it via streaming, because even in the same country two different providers have rights for different delivery methods!?! Rights deals are really, really complicated and the contracts are very complicated to go with that. It's usually all about the money!

Question: How do satellite TV and IPTV handle issues of latency and buffering, and which typically offers a more seamless viewing experience?
Answer: Satellite doesn't really ‘handle’ latency, it's an organic part of the encoding and the fact the signal must travel huge distances to space and back. Multicast IPTV can have pretty low latency but encoding still has some latency that cannot really be avoided. Commercial OTT streaming has been striving to improve latency with various Low Latency initiatives but adoption has been low because the systems don't usually scale that well. The compromises you need to implement true low latency make it difficult to justify commercially. But in some businesses low latency streaming is thriving because they find it beneficial.

Question: I watched the same show on cable and streamed on Prime on the same TV. I have 500 mbs internet. Why is the voice track clearer on cable than streamed?
Answer: It's probable that you are hearing the difference between a good stereo mix and a poor surround downmix. This is increasingly a problem with TVs and I also suffer from it from time to time. With simple stereo you're generally going to get a good mix with clear speech (unless someone screwed it up). But with surround sound, sometimes the vocal component, which is typically in the centre channel, can get poorly output by TVs. My advice would be to check the audio settings on your TV and see if you can switch the surround settings on and off. Even if you don't have surround, that'll be why.

Question: Did you know "free health care" in Britain comes with strings attached? Their waiting list is months long while in America you can see a doctor right away. British people, how do you feel about risking your life and your loved ones over mere money?

Eventually she was transferred to a nursing home, which turned out to be her final stop because after a month there she passed in her sleep from complications relating to her dementia. She'd worked pretty much her whole life. She paid her taxes (likely roughly the same percentage as the average American) and her care for the final months of her life was exemplary. She had 24/7 nursing care, from skilled people who cared greatly for her needs and made sure that despite her confused state she was not distressed. That care came with no strings attached, no financial burden on us or her at a difficult time. There was a discussion for a while that if she recovered she'd need to be in a care home and if her needs weren't severe, we'd have to pay. But if her on-going needs were medically essential, she'd have that paid for. There was never any decisions about withdrawing care, there was only a discussion about what was best for her needs going forward. My son was born 9 week premature, that's a very dangerous time and he spent a month in neonatal intensive care. Then he had at least two years of follow-up visits with a specialist and pediatric surgeon. He also had regular respiratory issues resulting in countless trips to the hospital, I might have been there every 20 days with him? He also needed special formula until he started solids. My greatest expense was paying for the parking at the hospital. He's a child, my financial situation shouldn't have an impact on the standard of care that he recieved. There was never a problem in getting an appointment for him with either a family doctor or specialist. I also have private healthcare insurance, it costs me less than $100 per month and has no exclusions for pre-existing conditions. I can use that to go to a private hospital if I want and I have done this. I had four visits to a specialist, a CT scan, abdominal surgery and I returned to the hospital every other day to have my wound checked. I think the surgery cost £2500? But I wouldn't know because there was no deductable for me to pay for any of it. How much would that cost where you are? I don't have to worry about mere money, it's not a consideration for my health.

Question: A lot of paid streaming services are tanking. Is this the same with free streaming services such as Tubi or Pluto TV?

There's a threshold of the number of services that people are willing to subscribe to and how much they will spend each month, so a portion of the audience who will watch a piece of content will just forget about it unless it's on the platforms they otherwise have. Not everyone who likes (not loves, likes) Marvel films will pay extra to watch them. So there's a lost generation by gatekeeping. Running the distribution infrastructure, the content management systems, the payment processing, the customer service system, the many app development teams AND the anti-piracy systems is expensive.

Name: Bob Hannent
Question: Why does the quality of Netflix appear lower compared to watching a Blu-ray disc of the same movie or show?
Answer: Netflix has to pay for the infrastructure that delivers the streams. They're relatively constrained in what they can deliver and ha e to put great effort into compressing the video as much as possible. They invented a whole system called VMAF to analyse the comparative quality of video (and made it available to anyone, which is nice). They encode the video multiple times, in multiple ways, and pick the one that produces the smallest file for the most balanced reduction in quality (because there must always be some loss). Blu-ray on the other hand, gets encoded with a huge bandwidth and very little compromise. There are some very long films that need to get compressed a bit more than average, but it could be argued that long films tend to focus more on the story than the visuals, or have less rapid motion that would put demand on the encoding (on average). Netflix funds a wide range of production and makes some good content. But their main selling point is convenience through variety on demand, not quality.

Name: Bob Hannent
Question: Is fiber broadband internet any better than satellite in rural areas?

Question: Are cable TV channels VHF or UHF?
Answer: I don’t know why so many people are asserting that cable TV isn’t VHF/UHF?! Yes, it’s not transmitted over free space but it’s still an RF signal, it just happens to live in a cable rather than air. It doesn’t stop being UHF just because it enters a cable, it also doesn’t stop being QAM just because it’s UHF. UHF and VHF are just definitions of frequency bands, they don’t describe the modulation scheme or the medium. Yes, digital or analogue, it’s still UHF or VHF. As for Cable networks, they have historically even delivered analogue radio in VHF over the cable! TV frequencies were also standardised in various places with different numbering schemes but in each case, there is a distinct difference in how VHF channels and UHF channels were allocated. Many cable networks followed these standards because the equipment they purchased assumes those standards. Increasingly we’re moving away from allocating everything to linear broadcast channels and allocating more channels to data. But until recently even most data channels used discrete broadcast channel allocations per carrier. Lately the carriers are getting more aggregated to allow more data to be put in a single carrier. So, the cable TV channels were, and still are broadcast in both VHF and UHF, there are channel allocations on most cable networks to account for this.

Question: When hosting a live event via satellite to a TV station, how are those usage charges and billed?
Answer: There are two ways that satellite contribution is charged: 1) If you’re using a VSat terminal which is based on internet connectivity then either you have a standard fixed plan for internet usage or you’re going to pay for the bytes transferred. This is increasingly the way that satellite contribution is going because it’s cheaper than the alternative and often the equipment sets itself up. With the likes of OneWeb and Starlink, I think this will be the way contribution happens in future. 2) If you’re using traditional “occasional use” satellite capacity then you’ll get allocated a frequency on the satellite which has an allowable RF bandwidth and you’ll book that for an amount of time. You’ll have a minimum booked time fee and then incremental blocks of time. For instance, minimum 30min, then 15min increments there after. If you finish early, you’re still paying for what you booked. If you need to over-run and you haven’t allowed enough time, you better hope no one is booked after you because there’s a chance the next person will put a spike through your signal. If you’re lucky someone can call the bookings line and get an extension for the over run. If you’re going to be running a long story or long running event, then you’ll get a discount for 24h, 1w, etc. If you’re a good customer who books often you’ll get a preferential rate. The bookings used to be done over the phone, I’ve been out of it for a while, so I don’t know if some of the companies have online scheduling systems now. We usually asked for an email or fax to confirm the booking as well, but calling up would ensure we had booked it in the system.

Question: Do DVB-T2 standard support satelite DVB-S2 and vice versa? If not, why do all TV makers ditching DVB-S2 first?
Answer: Satellite signals generally use PSK modulation and terrestrial signals use a more complex form of QAM. Satellite signals are very much more subject to noise because they get huge amounts of attenuation over the massive distances they're sent (and wide distribution). Terrestrial signals are less prone to this and have stronger signals, but they're subject to a great deal of reflection and instantaneous noise. They implement not dissimilar techniques but they come at it from a very different objective to deal with very different environments. Importantly, the chips are optimised to fixed function. Making the processing be more flexible means making them more complex. Additionally, if you add components for dealing with driving the satellite LNB, you're spending money and if it's not going to be used, that's money for nothing. In most countries, satellite TV is exclusively pay TV and heavily dependent on a separate set-top box. So the use of satellite for TVs directly is limited. Question: Why do I get no signal window when I get perfect picture on Samsung TV (dvi to hdmi)?
Answer: Sometimes a display shows a picture AND an error when there’s something wrong with the input video that the TV can’t quite understand. It’s more of a bug than a failure. In this case, it’s probably some kind of communication issue between the TV and the source device. With DVI and HDMI there’s a process called EDID where the sink (the TV) talks to the source and asks it what formats it supports. Then the response is used to decide how to display the video signal that gets sent. If the TV doesn’t like the EDID or the source offers formats that it doesn’t think it can display, it’ll put an error on the screen. But if so, why is it displaying a picture? Because the brains of the TV think it cannot, but the actual display processor, which is a separate component, somehow managed it. Or because the picture isn’t as perfect as you might think. For example there might be timing and alignment issues which you haven’t noticed and the TV is making a best effort at displaying it but it knows the video is being clipped (for example) or some other artefact is happening. It could just be that the source is sending no EDID, or the EDID is corrupt and the TV is showing an error because of this, but the display processor is happily showing whatever it found.

Question: Are the police called when there is a fight in a pub in the UK?

I’m not your typical guy to get involved in a skirmish, I’m not particularly tough, but ‘for the peace of the kingdom’ it was the right thing to do. You might ask why I didn’t detain them for the police? Well, “better out than in” and I didn’t want to be accused of anything like assault or detaining a person against their will. Plus it gave me a great story to tell about that time I broke up a bar fight. So yes, if you start a fight there’s a good chance the coppers will get called. Question: What makes the quality of a television so much better?
Answer: 1) The video scaling algorithms in the chipset play a big part in how the picture is rendered to the display. Question: Does my satellite dish/LNB (Bell) draw any power if it remains connected through a coaxial cable to our house, even if I don't have a satellite TV receiver box, and I use a different provider & technology (Rogers cable) for TV/Internet connectivity?
Answer: An LNB consumes about 1.5–2.5W when attached to a satellite box which is actively using it (e.g. if the box is on OR in active standby). If the box is in deep standby or switched off the LNB is as dead as a dodo. The LNB, if on all the time (some STBs do this) would cost you about 1c per day to run in energy. The average satellite receiver will consumer 0.5W in deep standby and perhaps 5–10W in active standby (including the LNB). A cable box, would not have the LNB power draw, but if it includes a modem that’s always on (as some do) then it’ll draw as much, if not more, than the LNB. I know lots of energy saving folk talk about turning things off at the wall when not in use, but honestly it’s not a big saving compared to other ways we waste energy.

Question: Will my 4K HDR TV automatically transfer my regular DVD's into 4K HDR?
Answer: Not really. Your TV has 4K resolution, it cannot display anything other than 4K because that’s the number of pixels that it has. When you watch a video that’s not 4K the TV has two choices, it can either display the lesser image at 1:1 pixel mapping and for SD that would put it as a small block in the middle of the screen, or it can scale that image up to fill the screen. That doesn’t make the DVD 4K, it just upscales the number of pixels and it doesn’t create any extra information because the DVD images contain all the information that’s being used to do that upscaling. There’s no magic that create extra data. Some TVs claim to do advanced AI upscaling and HDR interpolation, but that’s just the chip on the TV imagining improvements which you might like. It might invent some picture and/or enhance detail, but it’s not doing it with more information than was in the DVD. Same goes for HDR, there’s a chance it can stretch the dynamic range to give the DVD video more “punch”, but ultimately the DVD doesn’t have the information in it to reliably create detail that wasn’t recorded to the disk. My LG OLED actually shows DVDs played on Xbox One which are surprisingly tolerable in quality (for SD) but they’re still coming from an SD source.

Question: What's the transfer technology used for video sharing (i.e. YouTube, Vimeo, Facebook live streams, etc.)? Simple HTTP? Something else?
Answer: Most video streaming delivery is done with HTTP(S), the video itself is cut into chunks (called segments) which the player fetches, one by one. There is a manifest, this is a text file which describes how to fetch the video, audio, captions, etc. It describes the timeline, any ad breaks and also describes any DRM/security. There’s not a substantial difference between live and on-demand, but the manifest is regularly refreshed and the timeline keeps moving forward, indicating new segments have become available. As with any technology, there is no one right way and there are several popular technology approaches used: HLS, DASH and Smooth streaming, but they all use HTTP underneath. While HTTP is popular for stream delivery, it’s used mostly because CDNs can be used to scale delivery well, where other technologies are harder to scale with current internet infrastructure. But while streaming is delivered from those sites, how the material gets to those origins from the source can vary substantially, especially between on-demand and live. The most common live contribution is via RTMP or Zixi, but many professionals are now also moving to RIST or SRT.

DVB is pretty much the main international standard for digital TV systems, aside from the various, not insubstantial, national standards (that break out of their home markets). The Japanese didn’t make a better TV system than the rest of the world, they made one that primarily aims to support their local electronics companies by being different. Lobbying more countries to adopt ISDB-T means Japanese companies get first call on those markets because few other companies can be bothered to make ISDB-T products. As a side note, I was kind of disappointed that the ATSC didn’t adopt DVB-T2 after they ran a trial of it some time back. Question: How much will it cost to start a paid satellite broadcast TV provider with like 60 channels?
Answer: I’ve been out of this for a while, but I’ll give some numbers for scale. You’re first going to need to lease the satellite capacity, that varies by market but you’re going to need to start thinking about $5m per transponder (which carries ~15 channels), and you need 4 of those, so $20m for the satellite capacity lease per year. Caveat: the price can vary substantially, it could be $1m per transponder per year or up-to $5m). Then you’re going to want transmission services from a provider or you’re going to build your own uplinks. You’re going to start spend $500k building one satellite uplink, but you’ll want two because you don’t want to have a single site failure risk. Or you can out-source that to another company who gives you the SLAs and you avoid having to hire/train the highly skilled satellite transmission staff (and get certification for that). So I think transmission is probably going to cost you $1m per year but there are various approaches. Then you’re going to want encoding and muxing for the channels. I’ll say $500k per year for that, but depending on how you do it, you could go cheaper or more expensive. Then you need fibre connectivity to get the video from the channels themselves, that varies substantially by provider, but lets say $20k per month because your satellite uplink isn’t located in an urban centre and you need 4x 10GbE at least, via diverse routes. You also need a payment management and subscriber management system. You need a Conditional Access System (~$1–3m per year?).

Answer: It’s important to note that there are different organisations using different definitions of UHD, so it’s not exactly clear, plus there is also “UHD-1” and “UHD-2” to talk about the second generation of UHD. Some definitions of UHD say that it’s anything above conventional Full HD. And this includes 1920x1080p50/59.94 as long as it has HDR because perceptually, the HDR adds more value to the experience than just throwing more pixels at the display. 4K in TV terms is of course 3840 x 2160, and so that’s UHD-1, then UHD-2 is 8K. HDR is optional for 4K and 8K in most UHD specs. Also the definition of how HDR is delivered is unclear. UHD also includes mentions of 120fps which is amazing to see by the way.

Question: Why, when you turn off your smart TV, does it remain on?
Answer: There are typically three modes for a digital TV device: 1) On 2) Passive Standby - The deepest sleep, everything shutdown and the device is usually only able to respond to the remote to wake it up, unless a timer has been set in the TV. Saves the most energy. 3) Active Standby - The screen has turned off but the processor is still mostly running. This is used because the TV is waiting for something or doing some task in the background (sometimes called housekeeping). Examples of things that need to be done: storing the programme guide, or updating other databases such as smart apps, checking for system updates or tuning updates, waiting for some kind of network wake up or interaction with a smartphone app. Many times when you press the “power” button on a TV to switch it off, it’ll turn off the screen and go to active standby, do what it needs to do and then when all the housekeeping is done it’ll go to passive standby. My LG goes to deep sleep, active standby after about 5–10min.

Question: With as laughably inaccurate as TV subtitles are lately, why not have a human oversee and edit them, paid for by the individual cable services?
Answer: Most inaccurate subtitles are those done in real-time, such as those for the news or sports. There are humans there but they have a couple of seconds to react and practically it's hard to correct. You accept it and move on, hopefully you didn't do anything embarrassing or slanderous. The other way subtitles are wrong is when automated transcribing is done using voice recognition and no one checks it for accuracy. Traditionally, most broadcast, scheduled, non-live content went through a QC process (quality control) intended to catch anything that was technically wrong with the show before airing it. But I am aware that many companies have cut back on QC on recent years to save money. Some of the transcription services are better and some are worse, there are better techniques with fewer mistakes and there are cheaper alternatives. With the pressure to provide access services to everyone, for everything, there's perhaps been a focus on quantity over quality. Another minor and thankfully rare aspect is when the material accidentally gets miss-assigned, and the wrong captions get attached to the wrong content. This has previously had hilarious results.

Question: Why set top box, modem and IoT hub cannot be integrated into one device?
Answer: It's been done, but it's not terribly advisable. The first problem is that the STB is usually tied to the TV provider and the modem to the ISP. That's okay if they are the same. The second part and I suspect the critical one, is the IoT software needs to be maintained by the provider. For interoperability they often need to say that you can only use their IoT devices with it, otherwise they have to support every small device vendor as well. >95% of customers won't use the IoT functionality, we are outliers, those who are enthusiastic about these things. So, as a service provider, you're investing heavily in support and software for a minority of your customers. Probably about 10–12 years ago, at all the trade shows the manufacturers were showing off these combined Gateway devices. But with most provides, once we discussed the cost with them they decided they wanted the cheapest modem and the cheapest STB. SO back the usual. I can recall, I think, two providers doing it, I don't know how successful it was for them because I didn't supply the hardware for it. But I know it wasn't easy to get to market.

Question: Is the OTT platform earning more than satellite TV?
Answer: It’s harder to make money on OTT but easier to get started and grow your business with internet delivery vs satellite delivery. Satellite delivery demands scale, you have to have the money to deposit to get the capacity, the money to get the distribution services, the money to get the specialist skills needed to create the right kind of media. There are companies who will do all these things for you, but for a price, so you need plenty of financing up front. With OTT delivery it’s very much Pay as You Go, your costs are less “up front” and you get better deals as your customer base grows rather than having to sign up for a multi-year deal at the beginning. But with OTT your costs scale with viewership, as people watch more your costs increase, so you have to balance the revenue and costs carefully. With satellite your costs are more fixed op-ex, and once you hit break-even you’re going to be making more and more profit as your viewership rises. Very few legal OTT platforms are profitable, the margins are tight, but it’s the growth opportunity and costs are going down as the market matures. You used to have to pay for infrastructure to be built, now it’s available off the shelf and PAYG. Anyone can launch an OTT platform now, that also makes it an increasingly diverse and competitive market.

Question: Is it possible for someone sitting in the broadcast room of any television channel to actually see a viewer who is seeing the live TV at the moment if they know the location coordinates and address of the viewer's home?
Answer: No. This is weird paranoia. I’ve worked for broadcasters, pay TV companies, ISPs and streaming companies, I have a full view of what’s possible and practical. What can we do? * If you’re subscribed to a streaming service, your viewing is being logged, i.e. we know what you watched, how long for and on what device. * Cable TV and Internet companies have a “return path” and they can log some viewing, but when I worked for an ISP and we had our own TV service, I could see what people were watching. But viewers were just account IDs, I knew nothing about them. I was only because I knew my own account number that I could look up my own STB and see what channels my wife was watching at home. * The people who have access to viewing data don’t normally have access to any ability to see account details (e.g. address). This is because of data protection laws and it’s only businesses that are negligent that don’t restrict access to customer data, those companies usually get caught out in the end. When I wanted to know anything vaguely specific about a customer (e.g. what exchange they are connected to) I’d have to ask permission from someone else. * Access to viewing data is useful to be able to ensure you’re getting a good quality of service. If you’re getting a poor quality of stream then you want us to fix it. If we were working blind then we have to assume you’re fine or you’d have to call us and we’d have to send someone out to see what you’re seeing. Measurement is useful to save you time. Again, finally, you, individually, aren’t interesting. You’re just a number on a table to most of us. When you have a problem we’ll look into it. Collectively you might form part of an audience and if that audience isn’t getting a great service we’ll also look into that because we want everyone to get a good experience. Do I care if you’re sitting there in your underwear eating cheatos and crying? No, I have better things to do with my life. Does the government spy on you? No. They don’t care about monitoring the uses of cheato dust.

Question: When a broadcasting authority allows a single frequency TV network, how does it work? Does it mean that people in some areas won't receive transmissions who would otherwise, but in other areas will where they wouldn't otherwise? E.g. London local TV.
Answer: Normally it’s a coordinated thing where you arrange the SFN to cover an area by multiple transmitters. It doesn’t allow for local channels, so you typically have one or more non-SFN multiplexes on other frequencies which carry local content. An SFN could be small, with small transmitters covering a relatively small area, but that’s probably not worth the effort. The main idea of an SFN is to cover an entire country with one frequency and use multiple transmitters to re-enforce the signal over the whole geography. It generally gives customers better coverage than if you used an MFN because you could have customers who are marginal for two regions, but with an SFN they may get an enhanced signal due to having the signal combined from both transmitters. The important thing is that in most countries there isn’t just one multiplex, there are usually enough channels to fill multiple multiplexes. An SFN means you get good national coverage but you don’t have the ability to insert local content, but its only on one set of channels. You can run SFNs and MFNs along side each other, one or more SFNs for channels which are national, then a traditional MFN arrangement for more regional content.

Question: How do you wire every room with CAT8 Ethernet (data wiring, DIY, and Ethernet)?
Answer: If this is for a house, would you? Cat-5 is of course obsolete, Cat-6 is a good idea but Cat-7 and Cat-8? Overkill for anyone except those who would just get a specialist cabling contractor to install it anyway. Let’s start with the comparison chart of the modern cabling standards: Do you foresee every room needing 40Gbps any time soon? Are all runs under 30m/100ft? Do you want to buy the specialist crimping tool that you need to provide the exact pressure that Cat-8 cables require? Will you be buying a Cat-8 cable tester to ensure that the cable has been made correctly? Look, I get the idea of future proofing, it’s attractive, but the fact is that you can say “well, 8K video is more than 10Gbps”, sure, it is, but no consumer devices will be expecting to push around 25Gbps because no one else is installing Cat-8 cables. Thus, you might find a use for it if you happen to be in the “data horder” class of computer users and you find yourself owning several 32 core computers dotted around your house. But ultimately this is a professional technology and consumer equipment won’t be doing that in the next decade or two. If you really want to future proof yourself then buy multimode optical fibre cables and run them in pairs to each room. They can easily run 40Gbps and are cheaper than Cat-8 in most circumstances. When the connection I had from my house to my workshop broke I replaced it with fibre and because I had the right hardware my house is linked to the NAS in my workshop via 10Gbps, but I never even get close to using that capacity. It didn’t cost me much to implement and didn’t require any special tools either. If this question is about an office, I think the same rule applies. If your business isn’t doing stuff with big data or video processing then you probably won’t be needing 10G, let alone 25/40Gbps. Network capacity requirements for offices to individual computers has barely changed in the past decade. We were installing 1Gbps a decade ago and now we’re just on the cusp of a few machines being sold with 2.5Gbps! Those with more specialist needs can install and use fibre, it’s cheap and simple to install from my experience (unless you need to splice it because for some reason you can’t use pre-terminated fibre). Some might argue about the cost factor, but the reality is that copper is now very expensive as a commodity and unless you are buying CCA cable (which wouldn’t pass stringent testing in the long term) then buying good quality twisted pair copper is now more expensive than your average pre-terminated fibre. I would always advise installing wired connections in any property (commercial or residential) and installing more than you think you need because circumstances change. But don’t go overboard, don’t just grasp for the highest number to keep up, sometimes higher specs are there for a different type of user and this is one of those occasions. Personally and professionally, I don’t see myself ever using Cat-8. Why? Because I’ll use DAC cables for short distances and fibre for long distances. Everything else copper will probably be Cat-6 until someone hands me Cat-7 that I didn’t ask for and hopefully didn’t have to terminate myself.

Question: How do you wire a deep cycle battery in parallel?
Answer: Positive to positive, negative to negative… Then the load/charge connections should be at opposite corners of the combined battery. So if you have two batteries you connect the positive to the positive of the first battery and negative to the negative of the second battery. If you have 5 batteries in parallel, then you connect the load to the positive of the first and the load negative, to the battery negative of the last battery. Ensure you have thick conductors bridging the batteries, sufficient to ensure there is no voltage drop between cells under load.

Question: Is a digital TV signal stronger than analog?
Answer: A digital Tv transmitter needs substantially less power compared to the analogue equivalent to achieve the same coverage. Addison ally the digital signal works better in marginal conditions but fails more dramatically at what we call the digital cliff edge. Some people experience worse signal because new transmitters may no have been built to exactly match the coverage of the old analogue ones. In some cases new towers or new antenna elements were used which changed things. Some people were living on the edge and not noticing they had poor signal, now they have poor reception in digital things fail worse. Ultimately most people have more choice and better quality images as a result of digitisation, in some circumstances they have been let down, that usually is a business decision not a technical fault. Finally, not everyone knows that there is such a thing as too much signal. If you are having issues it is worth looking at whatever signal meter your TV is built with in the tuning menu. You can often see two bars, quality and signal level, signal level is relatively secondary to quality. Too much level can saturate the receiver and hurt the quality of reception. I had to remove an aerial amplifier after digitisation because of this issue.

Question: Why is streaming sports online not as smooth as watching sports through cable TV?
Answer: Broadcast delivery is done with one signal to everyone, one copy of the bits to everyone and it is done with error correction information sent along with the video. With Internet sports streaming every user is getting their own unique stream, their own transaction and generating their own traffic. The problem is the Internet isn't smooth, it's inconsistent and contention for bandwidth happens significantly more when it's a popular event. I work for a large streaming company, when we launched in Italy the entire Italian Internet shifted by a significant measure. If the Internet demand in a country changes during a game, for instance there is a new update for a computer game by Microsoft, then that can stretch the ability of ISPs and content delivery networks to cope. We work tirelessly to try and make things perfect, we want everyone to get a great experience. But we don't control the delivery end-to-end, as the cable companies do. The cable companies own everything from the encoder to the HDMI output on the set-top box. But, we are also unencumbered, unencumbered by legacy infrastructure and our economies scale work better in many ways because our costs go down when people don't watch and rise less than proportionately when many do. As technology improves we are optimising and improving delivery, there are teams of people working on that as their job. We are also working closely with Internet service providers (including cable companies) to make a better path for our traffic in their networks.

Question: What is the technical limit or capacity for cable television systems?
Answer: It depends on the legacy that the company is dealing with, ultimately if they can avoid legacy there is pretty much no practical limit to their capacity anymore. That might sound crazy but the cable spectrum for Docsis 3.1 is about 1.5GHz, and using 4096-QAM every 96MHz block in there can give over 900Mbps. That's more than 100 HD channels per multiplex and you can easily have 15 multiplexes to give you 1500 HD channels. But even if you think 1500 isn't enough, some big cable operators are moving away from traditional QAM+TS delivery and are moving to Multicast delivery. This means you could have over 17GBps per street cabinet and so everyone can watch whatever they want and instead of the channels being broadcast to everyone on the cable network each cabinet can decide what channels to carry based on the demand from customers at any moment. So in terms of TV, there are little or no limits left. If the operator hasn't been upgrading their network then I would suggest the limitations are much greater and depend on the implementation.

Question: Why are so many TV channels behind in resolution? Everyone I know own a 4k TV, and a lot of online media content creators make 4k content with a way smaller budget.

Then you need to upgrade the transmission suites to have 4K monitoring and to upgrade all your connectivity to deal with 4x the signal. Then, if most of your content is still HD, and only primetime content is in UHD you are broadcasting with 4x the bitrate than is necessary just for the quality at prime time peak. Look at daytime TV and ask me if that is justified being in 4K? So, you need to double your facilities at great expense because the equipment is premium. And then what? Studies have shown that consumer emotional engagement caps out at 1080p. Other studies have shown that 1080p+HDR has about the same value to consumers as 4K, and 1080p+HDR+HFR can even exceed 4K in perceived value in blind testing. Question: How has TV picture quality increased from the 1960’s to 2020?
Answer: Let's start with just resolution… That's a big difference alone. Then we have colour, the chroma subsampling of NTSC is about half that of modern digital TV. There is no comparison between old NTSC and UHD with HDR and WCG, that's akin to a cinema film in quality. NTSC, unlike PAL and Secam used elsewhere in the world, had an issue with colour accuracy which is why it has the alternative moniker of Never Twice Same Color. Also there was more noise in the production chain and cameras weren't nearly as sensitive in the 60s if they were tube cameras. If the show was recorded on film then its possible its between HD and SD if it was shot in 16mm which is why older shows can be recovered to HD if the original film copies remain. In terms of transmissions, with analogue you had more ghosting caused by signal reflections and more noise from interference. With digital you still get break-up but instead of declining quality as interference increases, digital TV works until it doesn't and then it falls off a cliff. This means you usually get good quality until you don't get anything.
